screens.title: Connecting to Redis with Popular Clients
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how applications connect to Redis using language-specific client libraries, why connection pooling matters, and how to handle common connection errors. We'll ground these ideas with hands-on examples in Python using redis-py and in Node. js using ioredis. You will see how hostname, port, and optional authentication are used in client configuration, how a simple ping confirms connectivity, and how set and get operate as request-response interactions. Understanding these basics helps you build reliable, low-latency applications that use Redis correctly. I'll also highlight practical pitfalls: hardcoded credentials, failing to close connections on shutdown, and not leveraging connection pools. By the end of this lesson you should be able to configure a client, perform basic commands, enable or verify pooling, and respond to connection failures with sensible error handling. Consider how a single unpooled client under heavy traffic makes every request wait for a fresh TCP handshake — a visible performance problem you can fix with pooling.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Connecting to Redis with Clients

Connecting to Redis with Popular Clients

Establish connections, run basic commands, and manage connection pools for reliable performance.

In this lesson
Client setup, PING/SET/GET, pooling and error handling.
Languages
Python (redis-py) and Node.js (ioredis).
Outcome
Run basic commands and configure pooling securely.
Coming up
Connecting

Host, port, and optional password to open a TCP session.

Pooling

Reuse connections to avoid handshake overhead on each command.

Errors

Detect and handle connection and auth failures gracefully.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Concept map

Client-Server
App sends commands, Redis replies over TCP.
Connection Pooling
A pool holds ready TCP connections for reuse.
Languages
Examples use redis-py and ioredis with practical snippets.
Quick tip
Avoid hardcoding credentials. Use environment variables and gracefully close the client on shutdown.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will practice during the chapter. First, you’ll be able to explain the client-server architecture for Redis and why TCP sockets and request-response semantics matter for correctness and latency. Next, you’ll configure and establish connections using redis-py and ioredis, including authentication and specifying host and port. You will implement basic Redis commands like ping, set, and get through those client libraries and confirm responses. Finally, you’ll recognize the importance of connection pooling, configure a pool, and use proper error handling to handle connection and authentication failures gracefully. Each objective is paired with a short verification step so you can test your competency. For example, a successful ping confirms connectivity, and a correctly configured pool shows that connections are reused under concurrent requests. As you work, watch for common misconceptions such as believing opening a new TCP socket per command is acceptable — it isn’t — and that client libraries always hide pooling details when sometimes you need to tune pool size for your workload.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to the technical setup, this chapter emphasizes safety and observability. You will learn to avoid hardcoding credentials by using environment variables or secret management, and to interpret client options such as decode_responses so your application deals with native string types instead of raw bytes. You will practice defensive error handling: catch ConnectionError or AuthenticationError in Python, and use error listeners and catch blocks in Node. js. You will also implement graceful shutdown behavior so the client pool is closed when your process exits. These practices reduce security risk and resource leaks and make your app easier to operate. For example, a missing decode option can cause surprising type errors when you treat returned bytes as strings; catching that early avoids runtime bugs. Throughout the exercises you'll annotate outcomes that verify each objective, such as a successful PING, proper decode behavior, and a pool that does not exhaust connections under load.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Learning Objectives — Safety

Security practices

Use environment variables for credentials and verify authentication behavior by attempting a connection without a password to observe failure modes.

Avoid
Hardcoded passwords, leaving clients open on shutdown, and ignoring decode options.
Do
Store secrets externally, set decode_responses when working with strings, and close pools on exit.

Observability

Log connection and authentication errors and monitor pool exhaustion to detect latency spikes early.

Checklist
  • Use environment variables for passwords.
  • Enable decode_responses in redis-py when returning text.
  • Ensure application calls client.quit() or pool.disconnect() on shutdown.

screens.title: Client-Server Model for Redis
screens.narratorSegment: Redis uses a classic client-server architecture: your application is the client and Redis is the server that accepts commands and returns responses. This interaction is built on network sockets, most often TCP, which creates an ordered, reliable stream for request and response traffic. It's important to treat each command as a request that expects a response; by default that request-response pair is synchronous on a single connection. For example, when you call Ping, the server replies with a simple acknowledgement; when you Set a key, the server stores it and responds with a status. A common misconception is to think Redis is in-process or automatically local; it is a separate server process, possibly remote, so network considerations like latency and firewall rules matter. Another subtle point is pipelining, where some clients allow batching multiple commands without waiting for each response immediately; that changes the timing model but still relies on the same TCP session. Understanding this model helps you reason about latency, concurrency, and why a pool of connections reduces repeated handshake overhead. Think about a web app issuing many short commands per request — without pooling each command might open a new TCP connection, which is costly. How will you validate the model in your own environment? Try a ping and observe round-trip time to see the network's role.

keyIdea.text: Commands travel over TCP between a client process and the Redis server; treat each as a request needing a response.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Client-Server Model
Definition

Client and server roles

A client sends commands to Redis; the server processes each command and returns a response over TCP. The pattern is synchronous per command unless pipelining is used.

Why it matters

Network latency affects operations, and treating Redis as a remote service helps you design retries and timeouts.

Common misconception

Redis is not automatically in-process. It runs as a separate server process and may be remote, so networking matters.

Process flow
Request-response sequence
  1. Client opens a TCP connection to host:port.
  2. Client optionally authenticates with a password.
  3. Client sends a command like PING or SET.
  4. Server processes and sends back a response.
Concrete example
A web app issues PING and measures latency. If server is remote, each PING includes network round-trip time; reducing socket creation by reusing connections lowers latency.
Key Takeaway

Treat each Redis command as a network request; reuse connections to limit repeated handshakes and latency.

screens.title: Connection Parameters and Authentication
screens.narratorSegment: To open a connection your client needs the server location and, when required, credentials. The core pieces are the hostname or IP address and the port number, which by default is 6379. If the Redis instance is protected, you must provide a password during client initialization so the server authenticates your session. Clients will attempt a TCP handshake and then perform any required authentication handshake. For example, redis-py accepts host, port, db, and password arguments when creating a Redis object; ioredis accepts these options in its constructor as well. A useful diagnostic step is an explicit PING after initialization: if PING succeeds you have an authenticated session and a working socket. A common mistake is to assume localhost implies the server is reachable — network namespaces, containers, or remote hosts may change that. Another mistake is hardcoding credentials into code; instead use environment variables or secret stores and read them at runtime. Finally, be aware that some client options affect returned data types, such as decode_responses in redis-py which converts byte responses to native strings; forgetting this can lead to type errors in your application logic. How will you verify authentication in your environment? Try connecting without a password and observe the expected AuthenticationError.

Parameters

Host, Port, DB, Password

screens.title: Basic Commands: PING, SET, GET (Python)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a small Python example that connects to Redis, pings the server, sets a key, and reads it back. The redis-py library exposes a Redis client object. When you construct it with host and port and optionally password and set decode_responses to true, your returned values are native strings rather than raw bytes. The sample code shows a try-except block to catch ConnectionError and AuthenticationError; this pattern prevents unhandled exceptions from crashing your application. After a successful ping, r. set stores a key and r. get retrieves it synchronously — the client waits for each response before sending the next command over the same connection unless you explicitly use pipelining. A practical example: set a 'session:user:42' key during login and then get it during request handling to load session data. A common mistake is to forget decode_responses and then treat returned bytes like strings, causing type errors. Another is to close the connection immediately in long-running apps; prefer letting pooling manage it, but ensure you close the pool at shutdown. Try running the sample and observe the printed values to confirm correct behavior.

keyIdea.title: Python example
keyIdea.text: Use redis-py to ping, set, and get; handle ConnectionError and AuthenticationError, and use decode_responses for strings.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Basic Commands — Python
Code Walkthrough

redis-py example

import redis
import os

REDIS_PASSWORD = os.getenv('REDIS_PASSWORD')

try:
  r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, password=REDIS_PASSWORD, decode_responses=True)
  r.ping()
  print('Connected to Redis!')

  r.set('mykey', 'Hello Cohortia!')
  value = r.get('mykey')
  print(f"Value for 'mykey': {value}")

except redis.exceptions.AuthenticationError as auth_err:
  print('Authentication failed:', auth_err)
except redis.exceptions.ConnectionError as conn_err:
  print('Could not connect:', conn_err)
except Exception as e:
  print('Unexpected error:', e)
This code uses decode_responses so get returns a string. The try-except pattern demonstrates graceful handling of connection and authentication failures.
Explanation
  • r = redis.Redis(...) opens a client using provided parameters.
  • r.ping() validates connectivity and authentication.
  • r.set and r.get are synchronous requests with immediate responses.
Key Takeaway

A simple ping and set/get verify both connectivity and expected data types when decode_responses is set.

Check your understanding

What happens if decode_responses is false and you try to concatenate a returned value with a string? Consider the type mismatch and how to fix it.

screens.title: Connection Pooling: Why and How
screens.narratorSegment: Connection pooling keeps a set of open TCP connections ready to use, rather than creating and tearing down sockets for every command. This saves the cost of repeated TCP handshakes, reduces latency, and lowers resource usage on both the client and server. A pool hands out an existing connection when your code needs to execute a command; when the command completes the connection is returned to the pool. Most modern Redis clients provide pooling either by default or through explicit configuration: redis-py manages a ConnectionPool under the hood while ioredis exposes pool behavior for high-performance use. A typical pool has a maximum size; if your application attempts more concurrent commands than the pool allows, requests will block or fail depending on configuration. A common error is to assume pools remove the need to tune concurrency — you still need to set an appropriate max_connections for your workload. For high-traffic web apps, inspect pool utilization metrics and increase pool size carefully, balancing available file descriptors and server limits. As a simple test, run concurrent requests and observe whether new sockets are created or reused. Pooling is the most effective first step to reduce latency from connection churn.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Connection Pooling
Definition

What a pool provides

A pool maintains open connections for reuse to avoid repeated socket handshake overhead and reduce latency under concurrent load.

Less latency
Reuse avoids repeated TCP handshakes.
Resource savings
Fewer sockets and lower CPU on the server.
Concurrency control
Pool size limits concurrent active sockets.
Scenario
A busy web server handling many requests will perform better if each request borrows a connection from a pool rather than creating a new socket. Monitor for pool exhaustion and tune max connections as needed.
Key Takeaway

Connection pooling is essential for high-concurrency systems to avoid excessive connection churn and latency spikes.

screens.title: Connection Pooling in redis-py
screens.narratorSegment: redis-py uses a ConnectionPool to manage sockets, and by default the Redis client uses an internal pool for you. You can create and configure a pool manually to set options such as max_connections. The pattern is to create a ConnectionPool, pass it into Redis, and reuse that Redis client across threads or request handlers. In the sample code we create a pool explicitly, create a Redis client backed by that pool, and then set and get keys to demonstrate usage. This explicit pool gives you control over max connections so you can tune for your workload. A common configuration mistake is leaving default max connections too small for bursty traffic or setting it too large and exhausting file descriptors. Also ensure that when your process exits you call pool. disconnect() or client. close() so sockets are released. For testing, simulate concurrent workers performing many sets and gets and observe whether the pool reuses connections instead of creating new ones. This gives measurable evidence that pooling reduces connection churn and improves request latency under load. Connection Pooling in redis-py means create a connectionpool and pass it to redis.redis to control max_connections and reuse sockets.. In practical terms, how redis-py manages a connectionpool and an explicit example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › redis-py Pooling
Code Walkthrough

Explicit ConnectionPool

import redis

pool = redis.ConnectionPool(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True, max_connections=20)
r = redis.Redis(connection_pool=pool)

r.set('anotherkey', 'Pooled connection works!')
print(r.get('anotherkey'))

# On shutdown
pool.disconnect()
Explicitly creating a pool allows you to tune max_connections. Use pool.disconnect() at shutdown to release sockets.
Notes
  • redis-py uses pooling by default but explicit pools give tuning control.
  • Set max_connections according to expected concurrency and OS limits.
  • Disconnect the pool on graceful shutdown to free resources.
Pro tip
Measure pool utilization under load to choose a sensible max_connections value rather than guessing.

keyIdea.text: Use ioredis to connect asynchronously, listen for connect/error events, and quit the client on shutdown.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › ioredis — Node.js
Code Walkthrough

ioredis example

const Redis = require('ioredis');

const redis = new Redis({ host: 'localhost', port: 6379, db: 0 });

redis.on('connect', () => console.log('Connected to Redis!'));
redis.on('error', err => console.error('Redis connection error:', err));

async function run() {
  try {
    await redis.ping();
    await redis.set('nodekey', 'Hello from Node.js!');
    const value = await redis.get('nodekey');
    console.log(`Value for 'nodekey': ${value}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Error executing Redis commands:', err);
  } finally {
    await redis.quit();
  }
}

run();
This async pattern uses event listeners and try-catch to handle errors. Call quit on shutdown so connections are closed gracefully.
Notes
  • ioredis handles pooling behaviors for many topologies internally.
  • Listen for error events to log and react to connection failures.
  • Call quit() on shutdown to free sockets and allow the process to exit.
Pro tip
Treat ECONNREFUSED as an operational signal: verify service status and firewall rules before retrying programmatically.

screens.title: Common Connection Errors and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When clients fail to connect you will see a few common errors. ConnectionError in redis-py or an error event in ioredis usually means the client could not open a TCP socket to the server. ECONNREFUSED indicates the target IP and port refused the connection, often because Redis is not running or a firewall blocks the port. AuthenticationError occurs when a password is required but not provided or is incorrect. Troubleshooting steps include verifying that the Redis process is running and listening on the expected port, attempting a local redis-cli connection to the same host, and checking firewall or security group rules that might block port 6379. Log useful diagnostics such as the host, port, and error message, but never log actual credentials. Common Errors
ConnectionError / error event
Indicates socket open failed; check service status and network reachability.
ECONNREFUSED
Server refused the connection — verify Redis is running and listening on the right port.
AuthenticationError
Password missing or incorrect; attempt a connection without password to observe the failure mode safely.

screens.title: decode_responses and Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: A small but important client option is decode_responses in redis-py. Redis stores bytes and returns raw bytes by default. When decode_responses is true the client decodes those bytes into native strings for you, which simplifies application code that expects text. If you omit decode_responses you will receive byte strings and may accidentally mix bytes and str types in your application, leading to type errors. Node. js clients commonly return strings by default, but it's important to check each client's behavior. This subtlety matters during input validation, serialization, and when interfacing with libraries that expect native string types. When writing tests, assert the returned type explicitly so you catch mismatches early. A misconception is to assume all clients handle decoding the same way; they do not. The defensive pattern is to set decode_responses when your application body expects text and to document that behavior for future maintainers. Definition

Client decoding behavior

redis-py returns bytes by default. decode_responses=True converts byte responses into native Python strings, avoiding common type errors in application code.

Concrete example
If you call r.get('key') without decode_responses you receive b'value'. Concatenating that directly with a normal string raises a type error unless you decode it manually.

Align client decode behavior with application expectations to avoid subtle type bugs.

screens.title: Security Best Practices and Secrets
screens.narratorSegment: Security is essential when connecting to Redis. Never hardcode credentials into source code. Instead read passwords from environment variables or a secrets manager at runtime. The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you through enabling a password in redis. conf and connecting with that password from both Python and Node. js. Test that an unauthenticated connection fails so you understand the AuthenticationError behavior. Use minimal logging for diagnostics and never print or persist passwords in logs. For deployments, ensure that network policies restrict which hosts can access the Redis port. Another practical point is to use separate databases or key namespaces per application when possible to avoid accidental data mixing. When you craft code for secrets, add a comment or README note explaining where credentials come from and how to rotate them. Finally, implement graceful failure behavior: if Redis authentication fails, fall back to a safe default or a degraded path rather than crashing the whole service. These steps make your application safer and easier to operate. Secrets and access control

screens.title: Graceful Shutdown and Resource Cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent operational issue is leaving connections open when a process exits, which can leak sockets and prevent clean restarts. For short scripts you may call client. quit() or pool. disconnect() at the end of the script; for long-running services you should hook into process exit signals and call the client's quit or pool disconnect methods during shutdown. In Python, call pool. disconnect() or client. close() depending on the client A P I; in Node. js, call redis. quit() to close connections and allow the process to terminate. Implementing a shutdown handler also allows you to flush buffered operations and avoid data loss. A common misconception is to think connection pools remove the need for explicit cleanup — they reduce connection churn but still require an orderly shutdown when the process stops. To test, start your app, then send a termination signal and confirm connections are closed on the Redis server side. This practice prevents file descriptor leaks and keeps operations predictable during code deployments and restarts. Graceful Shutdown and Resource Cleanup means always call client.quit() or pool.disconnect() on exit to release sockets and prevent resource leaks.. In practical terms, ensure clients and pools are closed when the application exits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Graceful Shutdown
Recommended pattern

Shutdown handlers

Hook into termination signals to call quit or disconnect and ensure open sockets are closed before exiting. This prevents resource leaks and keeps Redis connection counts stable.

Test
Send a termination signal to your app and verify that the Redis server shows the connection closed. If not, add explicit quit/disconnect calls in your shutdown sequence.
Example steps
  1. Register a shutdown handler for SIGINT/SIGTERM.
  2. Call client.quit() or pool.disconnect() inside the handler.
  3. Await completion before exiting the process.
Key Takeaway

Graceful shutdown prevents resource leaks and makes rolling deployments safer and more predictable.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core concepts to keep in mind as you work with Redis clients. First, client-server: your application is a client sending requests and receiving responses from the Redis server over TCP, and you should treat each command as a network operation. Second, a client library is a language-specific package that abstracts the network details and provides convenient APIs for commands, configuration, and pooling. Third, connection pooling maintains a set of open sockets to reduce handshake overhead and improve latency under concurrent load. These ideas connect: the client library implements the pooling that optimizes the client-server request cycle. When you practice, verify connectivity with PING, test SET and GET for data correctness, and observe pool behavior under concurrent requests. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how applications connect to Redis using language-specific client libraries, why connection pooling matters, and how to handle common connection errors. We'll ground these ideas with hands-on examples in Python using redis-py and in Node. js using ioredis. You will see how hostname, port, and optional authentication are used in client configuration, how a simple ping confirms connectivity, and how set and get operate as request-response interactions. Understanding these basics helps you build reliable, low-latency applications that use Redis correctly. I'll also highlight practical pitfalls: hardcoded credentials, failing to close connections on shutdown, and not leveraging connection pools. By the end of this lesson you should be able to configure a client, perform basic commands, enable or verify pooling, and respond to connection failures with sensible error handling. Consider how a single unpooled client under heavy traffic makes every request wait for a fresh TCP handshake — a visible performance problem you can fix with pooling.

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice during the chapter. First, you’ll be able to explain the client-server architecture for Redis and why TCP sockets and request-response semantics matter for correctness and latency. Next, you’ll configure and establish connections using redis-py and ioredis, including authentication and specifying host and port. You will implement basic Redis commands like ping, set, and get through those client libraries and confirm responses. Finally, you’ll recognize the importance of connection pooling, configure a pool, and use proper error handling to handle connection and authentication failures gracefully. Each objective is paired with a short verification step so you can test your competency. For example, a successful ping confirms connectivity, and a correctly configured pool shows that connections are reused under concurrent requests. As you work, watch for common misconceptions such as believing opening a new TCP socket per command is acceptable — it isn’t — and that client libraries always hide pooling details when sometimes you need to tune pool size for your workload.

In addition to the technical setup, this chapter emphasizes safety and observability. You will learn to avoid hardcoding credentials by using environment variables or secret management, and to interpret client options such as decode_responses so your application deals with native string types instead of raw bytes. You will practice defensive error handling: catch ConnectionError or AuthenticationError in Python, and use error listeners and catch blocks in Node. js. You will also implement graceful shutdown behavior so the client pool is closed when your process exits. These practices reduce security risk and resource leaks and make your app easier to operate. For example, a missing decode option can cause surprising type errors when you treat returned bytes as strings; catching that early avoids runtime bugs. Throughout the exercises you'll annotate outcomes that verify each objective, such as a successful PING, proper decode behavior, and a pool that does not exhaust connections under load.

Redis uses a classic client-server architecture: your application is the client and Redis is the server that accepts commands and returns responses. This interaction is built on network sockets, most often TCP, which creates an ordered, reliable stream for request and response traffic. It's important to treat each command as a request that expects a response; by default that request-response pair is synchronous on a single connection. For example, when you call Ping, the server replies with a simple acknowledgement; when you Set a key, the server stores it and responds with a status. A common misconception is to think Redis is in-process or automatically local; it is a separate server process, possibly remote, so network considerations like latency and firewall rules matter. Another subtle point is pipelining, where some clients allow batching multiple commands without waiting for each response immediately; that changes the timing model but still relies on the same TCP session. Understanding this model helps you reason about latency, concurrency, and why a pool of connections reduces repeated handshake overhead. Think about a web app issuing many short commands per request — without pooling each command might open a new TCP connection, which is costly. How will you validate the model in your own environment? Try a ping and observe round-trip time to see the network's role.

To open a connection your client needs the server location and, when required, credentials. The core pieces are the hostname or IP address and the port number, which by default is 6379. If the Redis instance is protected, you must provide a password during client initialization so the server authenticates your session. Clients will attempt a TCP handshake and then perform any required authentication handshake. For example, redis-py accepts host, port, db, and password arguments when creating a Redis object; ioredis accepts these options in its constructor as well. A useful diagnostic step is an explicit PING after initialization: if PING succeeds you have an authenticated session and a working socket. A common mistake is to assume localhost implies the server is reachable — network namespaces, containers, or remote hosts may change that. Another mistake is hardcoding credentials into code; instead use environment variables or secret stores and read them at runtime. Finally, be aware that some client options affect returned data types, such as decode_responses in redis-py which converts byte responses to native strings; forgetting this can lead to type errors in your application logic. How will you verify authentication in your environment? Try connecting without a password and observe the expected AuthenticationError.

Let's walk through a small Python example that connects to Redis, pings the server, sets a key, and reads it back. The redis-py library exposes a Redis client object. When you construct it with host and port and optionally password and set decode_responses to true, your returned values are native strings rather than raw bytes. The sample code shows a try-except block to catch ConnectionError and AuthenticationError; this pattern prevents unhandled exceptions from crashing your application. After a successful ping, r. set stores a key and r. get retrieves it synchronously — the client waits for each response before sending the next command over the same connection unless you explicitly use pipelining. A practical example: set a 'session:user:42' key during login and then get it during request handling to load session data. A common mistake is to forget decode_responses and then treat returned bytes like strings, causing type errors. Another is to close the connection immediately in long-running apps; prefer letting pooling manage it, but ensure you close the pool at shutdown. Try running the sample and observe the printed values to confirm correct behavior.

Connection pooling keeps a set of open TCP connections ready to use, rather than creating and tearing down sockets for every command. This saves the cost of repeated TCP handshakes, reduces latency, and lowers resource usage on both the client and server. A pool hands out an existing connection when your code needs to execute a command; when the command completes the connection is returned to the pool. Most modern Redis clients provide pooling either by default or through explicit configuration: redis-py manages a ConnectionPool under the hood while ioredis exposes pool behavior for high-performance use. A common error is to assume pools remove the need to tune concurrency — you still need to set an appropriate max_connections for your workload. For high-traffic web apps, inspect pool utilization metrics and increase pool size carefully, balancing available file descriptors and server limits. As a simple test, run concurrent requests and observe whether new sockets are created or reused. Pooling is the most effective first step to reduce latency from connection churn.

redis-py uses a ConnectionPool to manage sockets, and by default the Redis client uses an internal pool for you. You can create and configure a pool manually to set options such as max_connections. The pattern is to create a ConnectionPool, pass it into Redis, and reuse that Redis client across threads or request handlers. In the sample code we create a pool explicitly, create a Redis client backed by that pool, and then set and get keys to demonstrate usage. This explicit pool gives you control over max connections so you can tune for your workload. A common configuration mistake is leaving default max connections too small for bursty traffic or setting it too large and exhausting file descriptors. Also ensure that when your process exits you call pool. disconnect() or client. close() so sockets are released. For testing, simulate concurrent workers performing many sets and gets and observe whether the pool reuses connections instead of creating new ones. This gives measurable evidence that pooling reduces connection churn and improves request latency under load.
